Today’s picks

A race is rated only when every runner carries all six inputs the model uses: price, form, official rating, weight, days since a last run, and jockey and trainer records. A card with a gap anywhere in the field is not rated, and the missing field is named under Not rated. A value every runner shares is filed, not missing: it cannot separate the field, so it scores a neutral 50 rather than refusing the race. Each pick carries the paragraph of filed numbers behind it: no reason that is not on the card is used.

Not rated

What the numbers mean

Rating is the weighted average of the six inputs, 0–100. Clear of 2nd is its margin over the next runner in the same race. Win % converts the ratings into chances across that field. Top 3 is the Harville sum of those win chances under standard place terms, not a separately fitted place model, and is shown only where the field is large enough to have a place market. This is a rating, not a guarantee.

Lays

A lay is a bet that a horse loses. This tab names the runner the six-input model rates last in every race it can rate, with what laying it would risk at the card price: the liability is the price minus one per unit staked. A race the model cannot rate is not shown at all; its gap is named on the Today tab and never filled here. The price is the archived racecard price, not an exchange lay price. A venue's own lay price, the money available at it and its commission are not in any feed this build holds, so the liability is what the card price implies, not a quote.

Lay record settled, from the archived card

Across 8 settled days the model laid 92 runners, its last-rated horse in every race it could rate: 90 lost (97.8%) and 2 won. Read on liability rather than strike rate: the winning lays return 90.0 units, the losing lays cost 19.0, and 3,218.6 units of liability were at risk at the card prices, so the net of +71.0 units is +2.2% of what was at risk. The largest single lay risked 259.0 units — 3.6 times the whole net. A strike rate is not a strategy: one winner at that price undoes the record. Liability is the archived card price minus one per unit staked; card prices are racecard prices, not exchange lay prices, and no commission or available money is modelled, so this is the model’s own reckoning, not a venue P&L. No bet is placed.

Smarkets lays

The same runner the Lays tab names — the one the six-input model rates last in every race it can rate — priced at the exchange rather than on the card. Smarkets is a betting exchange, so the lay price is the highest resting bid and the liability is the lay odds minus one per unit laid. The quotes come from the anonymous public API and are delayed, so a price here is a snapshot, not an order: no stake is taken and no bet is placed. A race the exchange does not list, or a runner with no resting bid, is left out rather than given a price.

In off order, one row per rated race whose model lay has a resting bid. The edge is the model's chance for the runner minus the chance the lay price implies, in points; a negative number is the model rating the horse less likely than the book. This is a projection, not a record — a thin pre-off book can quote far from the card, and the liability column is what taking the price would risk, so one losing lay at a big price is the whole profile. The results tab is where it is judged.

Model chance audit — the twelve-factor record against the record

Across 263 settled GB/IRE races (2026-11-12 to 2026-11-22) the pick was shown at 27.0% and won 78 (29.7%, 95% CI 24.5-35.4%, a half-width of 5.5 points). The interval contains the stated figure.

Not yet informative: needs 87 more settled races. The 5 points between the 0.04 and 0.0498 scales over 246 matched races sit against the +/-4.8 points this sample would still carry at 350 races; the interval at that size is about the size of the gap, so it catches a gross error and only just begins to tell the scales apart.

Model notes 12 November build · superseded by the six-input model

These notes describe the twelve-factor rating that was live on 12 November. The weights below are that old set; the page no longer scores or picks with them.

  • The rebalance was tested before it shipped. Form drops from 24 to 15, official rating rises from 10 to 15 and Topspeed from 8 to 12, and the whole set was re-run over these 21 races. Winners found stayed at 11, but the winner now sits in the top five 19 times instead of 18 and the top pick placed 15 times instead of 14. Heavier versions were worse, not better: rating 22, form 10 and Topspeed 18 found only 9 winners.
  • It is a favourite-follower. The sheet's top pick won 11 of 21 races; the starting-price favourite won 13. On today's evidence you would have done better backing the shortest price than following this model.
  • Every winner it missed was 5/1 or bigger — 5/1, 11/2, 17/2, 11/1 and 18/1 — and in two of those five it had the winner 6th or worse in the field (the others were 4th, 4th and 5th of their fields). The improving longshot is the blind spot.
  • The factors that would have found them are the ones it trusts least. Diamond Grace took the Market Rasen 15:01 at 17/2 scoring 93 of 100 on official rating and 89 on Topspeed, but only 33 on the rating factor and nothing from the tipsters. Even after the rebalance it was only 5th of 8: official rating now carries 15 of the weight and Topspeed 12, against 13 for the rating and 15 for form.
  • It ranks fields well and picks winners poorly. The winner was in its top three 16 times out of 21, and in its top five 19 times, but its top pick won only 11. The ordering near the head of a race is noisier than the ratings suggest.
  • A scoring bug was live in the morning sheet and is fixed. The tipster factor could go negative for horses nobody tipped (as low as −300), pushing unbacked runners down harder than intended. Correcting it reordered at least two races: total winners fell from 12 to 11, and at Thurles 15:15 the 18/1 winner Duke Otto dropped from 3rd to 8th. The corrected model is, if anything, more of a favourite-follower — so the verdict above is not flattered by the fix.

Longshot results

Every longshot the model flagged on a settled day it could rate: a card price of 7/1 or bigger, a top-four model rank, at least a 4% win chance, and a model chance above the price’s implied chance. Rows are read off the same six-input re-score as the ledgers, so a race with a gap in its card is left out rather than filled in. A row enters only when the stored result names the horse: nothing is re-scored after the fact. Prices are the archived card prices, not a quote.

Across 8 settled days the screen flagged 149 longshots: 6 won (4.0%) and 143 were beaten. The stored result names the first three home, so a beaten longshot shows a placing only where it is named there and a dash otherwise; 21 were in the frame. Each row would have been one unit at the archived card price. No stake is taken and no bet is placed.

How the rating works

Six inputs, fixed weights, one score per horse — and only on a card where every runner carries all six. Nothing is tuned per race or per horse, so two identical profiles always get the same rating.

How the rating is calculated

Each input is scored 0–100 and averaged with fixed weights. The six entries and 56 nominal weight are fixed: nothing is user-adjustable and nothing is dropped per horse: if one runner is missing one input, the race is not rated at all. That is why the model runs on six inputs rather than a dozen. A factor can only enter the model if the feeds file it for every runner; the ones that are patchy are excluded for the whole page rather than for the horses that happen to lack them.

Market (18)
Implied probability from the price with the book's margin removed, so the field's shares sum to 100.
Form (15)
Last six finishing positions, most recent weighted heaviest, blended 65/35 with how often the horse hits the frame. No top-three finish in its last six caps it at 55; one run caps it at 68, two at 76; no form scores 30.
Official rating (15)
The handicapper's rating, normalised across the field.
Weight (2)
Lower weight scores higher — the point of a handicap.
Days since a run (3)
Days since last run: peak at 15–35, penalised for long absences and quick reappearances.
Jockey & trainer (3)
The win counts printed against the jockey and trainer on the card.

Not model inputs, and why: Racing Post ratings, Topspeed, tipster counts and naps, the course/trip/going flags and the draw. They are not filed for every runner on every card, so they cannot be carried into a rating without a horse being scored on less evidence than its rivals. Rather than drop them per horse, the race is left unrated and the missing field is named on the Today tab. If those feeds become complete, they can enter the model with a weight, not before.

The paragraph on each pick is generated from the card's own values: the price and its share of the book, the form string and what it contains, the official rating and its distance from the field high, the weight carried, the days since a run, and the jockey and trainer win counts. It also states the rating, the margin over the second-rated horse, the win chance and the top-place chance. No sentence is written that is not backed by one of those values.

Top places: the place chance is the Harville sum of the model's own win chances for that field, shown only where field size gives standard place terms. It is arithmetic on the win model, not a separately fitted place model, and it is labelled that way on the card.

Hong Kong market: HKJC cards are filed before betting opens, so a Hong Kong pick is scored on the factors the card carries and not on the price. Win odds are now archived from twenty minutes before each off; none has been filed yet, so no Hong Kong market factor can be tested.

The Model percentage: the 0–100 rating turned into a win chance across the field (a softmax with a fixed scale of 0.04, fitted on 2,251 held-out races). It is a display figure: the selection is still the highest rating, and the ranking does not move with it.

What this is not: a forecast. It has no sectional times, no video, no gallops reports and no stable information. It applies the same reasoning consistently to every runner on the card — it does not make it correct.

Race Sheet is a fixed-weight rating model. Cards and results refresh automatically; the Model percentage is a calibrated win chance from the model's own rating, not a bookmaker probability, and the Market column is the chance the price implies.
